---
title: The nature of behavioral data
subtitle: The terms used to describe data, and what they mean in BDM
aliases: [/explanations/data.html]
---

Data is described with words that indicate how it was collected, stored, organized, or processed. Those words are used loosely in practice, and the looseness matters: whether a dataset counts as "raw" determines what may legitimately be done with it. This page sets out what each term means in BDM.

## Raw and derived

Data that has not been processed is **raw**; data computed from other data—summary statistics, scores, fitted models—is **derived**. Reproducible research requires sharing the raw data alongside the analysis code, so that others can replicate the whole chain rather than inspecting its conclusions.

The boundary is less obvious than it appears. In BDM, data stops being raw once it has been processed in a way that reflects an assumption about what the values mean. Filtering out trials with response times under 150 ms, on the belief that such responses cannot be genuine, is such an assumption: the result is no longer raw. Removing duplicate records written twice by a logging bug is not, because no scientific judgment is involved.

The following operations therefore preserve raw status:

- selecting variables;
- renaming variables and enum values;
- converting units (e.g., milliseconds to seconds);
- reordering rows and columns;
- removing duplicates;
- joining or splitting tables.

## Native and tidy

Systems record data in whatever shape suits them—structured or not, as CSV, JSON, MAT, or a proprietary format. That is data in its **native** format. **Tidy** data is organized so that each row is an observation and each column a variable.

BDM datasets are tidy. The rules a table must satisfy, and the row and column ordering that goes with them, are specified in [Tables](/spec/conventions/tables.qmd).

Note that native and raw are independent: data in its native format often contains derived values (a total score stored alongside the individual responses), and native data may happen to be tidy already.

## Database and dataset

A [**database**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Database) is a collection of data managed by a database management system, implying ongoing interaction: users read and write to it.

A [**dataset**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_set) is also a collection of data, but a static one—downloadable and shareable as a whole, like the [PISA 2012 dataset](https://www.oecd.org/en/data/datasets/pisa-2012-database.html). A dataset may be defined by a collection campaign (everything gathered in a project) or by an analysis campaign (a subset extracted from a larger database for one purpose).

BDM describes datasets. The catalog that a collection of datasets forms is a separate concern.

## Storage architectures

A [**data lake**](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/DataLake.html) is an unstructured collection of data from many sources. It is maximally flexible—tables in any format, images, text—which is also its weakness: without structure it degrades into a data swamp.

A **data warehouse** organizes incoming data consistently before storing it (schema-on-write), so its contents are ready for analysis. The cost is that everything must be shaped on the way in.

A **data lakehouse** combines the two: the flexibility of a lake with a semi-structured layer applied on read, giving quick access without demanding that every source be normalized up front. This is the architecture BDM is designed for, and the reasoning is developed in [Design process](design-process.qmd).

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
A [**data mart**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_mart) is a subset or view of a warehouse, optimized for a particular use or audience.
:::

## What to store, and what to share

More data is stored than shared. A study may hold participants' contact details or hardware parameters that will never be published.

What to *store* depends on the study, subject to two constraints: participants must be informed what is collected, and collection must follow the applicable regulations. Being parsimonious with personal data is generally wise (see [Datensparsamkeit](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/Datensparsamkeit.html)).

What to *share* is a different question. In BDM, native-format data should not be shared when better-formatted data can be extracted from it, for three reasons:

- **Usability.** Native data is often messy, sometimes in proprietary formats, and rarely documented.
- **Privacy.** Native data may contain personal information the sharer is unaware of—full names, IP addresses. Defining what will be shared, and extracting only that, avoids accidental disclosure.
- **Responsibility.** Preparing usable data from a native recording is the data engineer's job, not the analyst's. Handing over both the native data and the extracted data transfers that responsibility: an analyst who can see the preprocessing code becomes accountable for errors in it. This does not remove the obligation to verify the extraction—it places that obligation with the party doing the extracting.

In short: do not share unformatted native data. Share well-documented, well-formatted raw data.

## Versioning

Datasets change as data is added and errors are corrected, so they need versions. Appending version labels to filenames raises more questions than it answers—whether to relabel every file, only changed files, or only the root—so BDM records the version in the dataset's metadata instead, where [schema.org](https://schema.org) and [CalVer](https://calver.org) provide the vocabulary and platforms such as [Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/) display it. For tracking the data itself across versions, [DVC](https://dvc.org/) is a reasonable choice.

See [Dataset cards](/spec/dataset-cards.qmd) for where the version is recorded.
